newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Korean prosecutors seek more arrests in loan furore.
newsitem.headline: Korean prosecutors seek more arrests in loan furore.

text.p: South Korea's loans-for-kickbacks scandal bit deeper into President Kim Young-sam's power base on Thursday as state prosecutors sought arrest warrants for a former cabinet minister and two lawmakers.
Home Affairs Minister Kim Woo-suk resigned on Wednesday, hours before prosecutors grilled him over his role in securing loans of $5.8 billion for failed Hanbo Steel Co.
The minister and one of the two lawmakers, Hwang Byung-tai, are presidential loyalists who lead a faction that backed Kim Young-sam's rise to power.
Hwang heads the powerful finance and economy committee in parliament.

The other member of the National Assembly is Kwon Roh-kap, a top aide to opposition leader Kim Dae-jung. Kwon has already admitted taking money from Hanbo Group founder Chung Tae-soo, who is now under arrest.
A senior prosecutor has said the three are under suspicion of taking kickbacks from Hanbo to secure loans for a new steel mill or silence criticism over the size of the loans.

On Tuesday, prosecutors arrested another veteran member of Kim's personal entourage, Hong In-gil, along with Chung Jae-chull, the highest-ranking official in the ruling New Korea Party after the president and the party chairman.
Both have been charged with taking backhanders.
Kim Young-sam's credibility as a social reformer has taken a fresh battering with every associate that falls foul of the investigation.
"Kim Young-sam is facing the worst crisis of his political life," an editorial in the Chosun Ilbo daily said.
"The Hanbo incident reveals the morality of President Kim Young-sam's close associates."
Kim took office in 1993 pledging to uproot corruption from a country whose "miracle" economy was built on a murky alliance between politicians, big business and banks.
He flushed out illicit wealth by insisting that bank deposits be stored under real names, and promoted honesty in government by forcing civil servants to declare their assets.
His assault on graft culminated in the trials and conviction for bribery and human rights abuses of his two predecessors, Roh Tae-woo and Chun Doo Hwan.
"Now his entourage is showing its second face," the editorial said.

Although President Kim personally ordered an investigation into how Hanbo Steel leveraged its net worth of $300 million to secure about $6 billion in loans, and has openly called it a graft case, his credibility is now on the line.

Kim cannot run for a second term in office, but with scandal swirling closer to him and his party's power centre he will have less room to manoeuvre as he seeks to anoint a successor to run in December's elections.
The home affairs minister was the third cabinet member to depart in less than six months under a corruption cloud.
Already, there are signs of factional in-fighting in the ruling camp as presidential candidates jockey for position.
